content.prompt: Implement binary search on a sorted array. Find the index of the target, or return -1.
content.hint: If arr[mid] < target, the answer must be in the right half — set left = mid + 1.

content.text: Sorting is like organizing a messy bookshelf — once sorted, finding anything becomes trivial. Binary search is the "guess the number" game: I think of a number between 1-100, you guess 50, I say "higher." You just eliminated 50 possibilities in one guess. Custom Comparator is like telling a librarian "sort by page count, not title" — same books, different ordering rule.

content.annotation: Binary search uses left + (right - left) / 2 instead of (left + right) / 2 to prevent integer overflow when left and right are large. The while condition is left <= right for exact match. Custom Comparator lambda (a, b) -> returns negative (a first), positive (b first), or zero (equal). Chain multiple criteria with if-else as shown in sortEmployees.

content.modification: What if we change `left = mid + 1` to `left = mid`?
content.question: What happens when searching for target = 9?
content.explanation: When left = 3 and right = 4, mid = left + (right - left) / 2 = 3. Since arr[3] = 7 < 9, we set left = mid = 3. Next iteration: same left, same right, same mid — the while loop never terminates. Setting left = mid + 1 ensures we skip the already-checked mid element, guaranteeing the search space shrinks every iteration.

content.question: When would you choose linear search over binary search?
options: When data is unsorted and you only search once
When the array is very small
When you need the last occurrence
content.explanation: Binary search requires sorted data. If you search only once, sorting costs O(n log n) plus O(log n) for the search — worse than a single linear O(n) scan. Binary search wins when you sort once via Arrays.sort and then call binarySearch many times — the O(n log n) sort is amortized across many O(log n) lookups.
